title: Finding community
hookLine: a synagogue, a study group, a Shabbat table, online or in person
tomorrow: Saba's minyan is one short. why does prayer wait for ten?

cards: A man wakes up under a rock ledge, stiff and starving, and something is wrong. The carob tree he watched someone plant is heavy with fruit, and a stranger is picking it.
The Talmud tells this about Honi, the circle-drawer. Before he lay down, he asked the planter why he'd bother with a tree that takes seventy years to bear.
The planter said: my grandparents planted for me, and I'm planting for my grandchildren. Then Honi slept, the story says, for seventy years. Now he's awake, and he walks to the study house he loved.

teach.b: The scholars are saying: these teachings are as clear as in the days of Honi. He tells them: I'm Honi. They don't believe him, and nobody greets him the way he was once greeted.
Everything he learned is still there. His people are gone.

The Talmud says he asked for mercy and died, and that people drew a saying from it, in Aramaic: o chevruta o mituta, either companionship or death. A hard ending, told plainly, about how much people need each other.

Hillel turned it into an instruction in Pirkei Avot: don't separate yourself from the community. Notice what neither text says. Neither says find the perfect community, or the one where everyone already knows your name.
Honi's trouble wasn't the wrong room; it was having no one.

So community, lived, can be small: a synagogue where you sit in the same row each week, a study group around a kitchen table, a friend's Shabbat dinner, a class on a screen full of little squares of faces.
Some people find theirs fast; some try a few before one fits. And the planter is the other half of the story. Somebody planted a community before you got there, so it would be there when you came.

how: Many Jews find community through a synagogue, a study group, a campus or community center, or regular Shabbat meals with friends; many synagogues welcome newcomers to services and meals.

o: choosing one synagogue and staying there for life
a city's official list of all its Jewish groups
going toward people who will know you, not waiting alone

p: slept and woke to no one he knew

s: in the Talmud, Honi's old friends welcome him back
they don't believe him. he asks for mercy and dies, and the saying drawn from it is: companionship or death.
Hillel taught not to separate yourself from the community
it's in Pirkei Avot, given as an instruction.
finding community means finding the one perfect synagogue
Honi's trouble was having no one, not the wrong room. a study group or a Shabbat table counts.

games.q: your cousin moves to a new city and says she'll look for a synagogue once she finds one that feels exactly right. by Honi's story, what's her best first move?
o: show up somewhere small this week and let people get to know her.
wait until she's sure, so she doesn't waste anyone's time.
pick the biggest congregation in town so she can stay anonymous.
games.why: Honi's ending is about having no one. the tradition's answer is to go toward people now; the fit grows from showing up.

practice: Name one community you could reach toward: a synagogue's newcomer table, a study group, a friend's Shabbat dinner, an online class.
Then name what usually stops you, a shy streak or a full week, and one step around it, an email or a time to show up. Hold that one plan while your breath slows.

wordCard.voice: Finding community: going toward people instead of waiting to be found. Honi woke to a world with no one in it; the tradition answers by sending you toward others.

orig.note: Hebrew: a community or congregation, the people gathered together.

carryVoice: Keep this one: find your people, the way someone once planted a carob tree for you. Day one of community and justice.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud Ta'anit 23a (Honi, the carob planter, the long sleep, the study house, 'either companionship or death')
Mishnah Avot 2:4 (Hillel: do not separate yourself from the community)
